summary: This Standards Track document defines the eap.arpa. domain, used only in Network Access Identifiers, so an EAP peer can ask the server for limited, unauthenticated network access. Predefined identifiers in the NAI format of RFC 7542 say what kind of access is wanted. It updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140, and RFC 9190.

eli5.summary: A visitor with no key tells the front desk, using a special visitor name, that they need to reach only the lobby.

questions: what is an eap provisioning identifier
subtitle: A reserved name that lets a device with no credentials ask a network for limited access, just to get provisioned.

tldr.problem: EAP normally needs pre-provisioned credentials, so a device with none cannot get network access to be provisioned. EAP-TLS allows unauthenticated access but defines no way to ask for it.
tldr.mechanism: Peers send a predefined identifier in Network Access Identifier format under the eap.arpa realm, such as portal@tls.eap.arpa. Servers recognize it and place the peer in a limited network such as a captive portal.
tldr.outcome: It creates an IANA registry of provisioning identifiers, starting with @noob.eap.arpa and portal@tls.eap.arpa, and updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140 and RFC 9190.

today: RFC 9965 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140 and RFC 9190, and deprecates the eap-noob.arpa name in favor of @noob.eap.arpa.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
In most uses, EAP (RFC 3748) requires that peers have pre-provisioned credentials. Without them a device cannot get network access to be provisioned with credentials. This is a bootstrapping problem.

The RFC creates a framework of predefined, well-known provisioning credentials. A client submits one to obtain limited network access, and the server knows in advance that it is for provisioning only, so it can avoid granting unrestricted access. The device can then provision over the EAP channel itself, as TEAP (RFC 9930) does, or the server can place it in a limited captive portal as in RFC 8952. Once provisioned, it uses the new credentials for full access.

The identifiers are called EAP Provisioning Identifiers (EPIs). Where the EAP method supports it, access is password-less; where a password is required, it is the same as the identity.
sections.eli5: A gadget that has never been set up cannot join the network, and it needs the network to get set up. This RFC gives it a special way in, just enough to finish setting up.

sections.title: What Existed Before
sections.content:
Both RFC 5216 (Section 2.1.1) and RFC 9190 provide for EAP-TLS "peer unauthenticated access", but define no way for a peer to signal that it wants it. The RFC says there appear to be no peer or server implementations that support such access. The Wi-Fi Alliance defined an unauthenticated EAP-TLS method in HotSpot 2.0r2, but there appear to be few deployments.

EAP-NOOB (RFC 9140) both signals that provisioning is wanted and exchanges the provisioning data inside the method. TEAP provides provisioning through an unauthenticated TLS tunnel, but its inner exchange requires both ends to authenticate.

The RFC sees two provisioning scenarios: provisioning inside the EAP method, and using EAP to get limited access and then running IP-based provisioning. Provisioning inside EAP matters because the AAA administrator often does not control the network, so a captive portal may not be possible.
sections.eli5: Earlier rules hinted that a visitor pass could exist but never said how to ask for one. This RFC fills in how to ask.

sections.title: The eap.arpa Realm and Identifiers
sections.content:
An EPI is a strict subset of a Network Access Identifier (NAI, RFC 7542) whose realm is a subdomain of eap.arpa.. The realm is chosen to be unused by any organization and not automatically proxied by AAA systems or discoverable by dynamic discovery. Existing implementations that see such an identity are expected to return EAP Failure, which makes the scheme fail-safe.

The subdomain under eap.arpa. says which provisioning method is wanted and is assigned via the EAP Provisioning Identifiers registry. Where possible the first subdomain SHOULD be the EAP method name. The username part depends on the method. It MAY be empty or fixed, and "anonymous" is NOT RECOMMENDED. Privacy is not needed because the names are in public specifications.

Every realm in the registry also implicitly defines a v. sub-realm, such as v.tls.eap.arpa. Vendors and standards bodies can self-assign there using domains they own, for example example.com.v.tls.eap.arpa. Experimental methods MUST use the vendor's own name space, and the IETF uses ietf.org.
sections.eli5: The special visitor name has two parts: who you are asking to be, and which door you are using. Everyone knows the names because they are written in a public list.

sections.title: What Peers Do
sections.content:
A peer signals the kind of provisioning it wants by sending an EPI together with the matching EAP method. The EPI MUST come from the registry, and the EAP method MUST match the registry entry. If users can choose a provisioning method, the peer picks the matching EPI itself. The peer MUST NOT offer an interface to type the identifier directly for provisioning, and it MUST NOT check whether identifiers users enter for ordinary methods match an EPI.

On success, new credentials are provisioned, the peer drops its connection and re-authenticates with them. It is RECOMMENDED that it try them immediately so errors surface quickly.

On failure, peers MUST track which methods they tried and not repeat one to the same server after an EAP Nak, and they MUST rate limit attempts. They SHOULD retry no more than once every few minutes with jitter and exponential backoff, and SHOULD err toward long delays, retrying after at least a day and perhaps no more than a month. Peers with expiring credentials SHOULD provision new ones before expiry, ideally through a re-provisioning method that works with full network access.
sections.eli5: The visitor says the special name, and if the desk says no, they do not keep shouting it. They wait a good while before trying again.

sections.title: What Servers Do
sections.content:
A server implementing this RFC MUST check whether the identity's realm is under eap.arpa. A malformed EPI MUST get an EAP Failure. An EPI the server does not recognize MUST get an EAP Nak of type zero, and so must a proposed EAP method the server does not support or does not accept for that provisioning method. When the server accepts, it replies with the EAP method that matches the EPI.

Servers MUST treat such peers as untrusted. Once authenticated, a peer MUST be placed in a limited network such as a captive portal, with no unrestricted access, and implementations should watch for bypasses such as tunneling data over DNS. A secure provisioning network allows only expected traffic and blocks all else. The limited network SHOULD also cap the duration of access (seconds to tens of seconds), the data transferred and the services offered. Servers SHOULD rate limit attempts and the number of peers provisioned at once. Peers in the limited network MUST be prevented from talking to each other.

Method negotiation is not permitted: any Nak sent with an EPI MUST contain only method zero, and a peer MUST ignore any methods in such a Nak. Servers using RADIUS dynamic discovery MUST NOT look up names in eap.arpa. in DNS.
sections.eli5: The front desk checks the visitor name. If it makes sense, the visitor gets a pass to the lobby only, with a timer, and cannot wander or chat with other visitors.

sections.title: Fitting Into EAP Methods
sections.content:
For password-based methods, the password SHOULD be the same as the provisioning identifier, and for TLS-based tunneled methods the inner identity and inner password SHOULD both be the identifier. Provisioning via a TLS-based method is RECOMMENDED, because TLS authenticates the server and protects the data.

Every provisioning method under eap.arpa. MUST define a way to authenticate the server, either in EAP or after access is granted, for example over HTTPS. A peer MUST still validate server certificates except for provisioning, and when provisioning happens over another protocol it MAY skip validating the EAP server certificate. Either way it MUST treat the local network as untrusted.

The RFC defines portal@tls.eap.arpa for unauthenticated EAP-TLS, signaling that the peer wants captive portal access. Peer unauthenticated access MUST still authenticate the server, so a TLS-PSK with a well-known key is generally not appropriate. For EAP-NOOB, servers are RECOMMENDED to accept both noob@eap-noob.arpa and @noob.eap.arpa, and peers to try @noob.eap.arpa first.
sections.eli5: Even a visitor should be sure they are talking to the real front desk. And since the visitor name is public, the secret word is just the name itself.

sections.title: IANA Actions and the Registry
sections.content:
IANA added eap.arpa to the .ARPA Zone Management registry and to Special-Use Domain Names, and marked eap-noob.arpa as DEPRECATED. DNS servers asked for eap.arpa. SHOULD return NXDOMAIN, and registrars should deny registering it.

A new registry, EAP Provisioning Identifiers, was created under the EAP registry group, with Expert Review. Entries give an NAI, a Method Type and a reference. The designated expert posts requests to the EMU working group list and decides within 30 days. NAIs SHOULD look like action@name.eap.arpa, MUST be lowercase and unique case-insensitively, MUST NOT have more than one subdomain, MUST NOT be "anonymous" and MUST NOT start with v.. Because RADIUS carries them in User-Name, they should be short: implementations are likely to support 63 octets in total, 63 to 253 may work, and 254 or more will not.

Self-assigned v. realms are for testing and future expansion, and organizations are RECOMMENDED to avoid them.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps all the allowed visitor names. A referee checks new names to make sure they are short, clear and not already taken.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC lets unknown, anonymous and unauthenticated devices obtain network access, so operators must provide only limited access. On-path attackers can succeed where they normally would not, because credentials are public and server validation may be skipped. Peers and servers MUST assume all data in the session is visible to and modifiable by attackers, and the methods MUST be used only to bootstrap initial access.

To secure the provisioning network, allow only traffic needed for the current method, offer only needed services, and limit simultaneous devices, per-device attempts, time on the network and data transferred. DNS recursive resolvers SHOULD NOT be available there, since DNS has been used to exfiltrate traffic.

On privacy, the names are public, so exposing them is harmless. The RFC changes neither EAP nor RADIUS, and says it can increase privacy by letting devices obtain access anonymously and then securely get credentials.
sections.eli5: Because anyone can be a visitor, the lobby has to be built as if some visitors are up to no good. Keep it small, timed and boring.
